Healthcare is increasingly seeing conversations around the integration of conventional medicine with traditional and complementary healing practices. Rather than viewing these as competing approaches, the focus is shifting towards understanding how different systems can contribute to patient care, while maintaining appropriate standards of safety and clinical evidence.

India has a long history of traditional healing practices, including Ayurveda and other AYUSH systems. However, their integration into mainstream healthcare continues to raise questions around scientific validation, clinical evidence, standardisation and the role of medical practitioners.

Interest in these practices is also growing internationally. Wellness tourism based on alternative healing, including Ayurvedic retreats and yoga centres, brought in approximately USD 22.61 billion to India in 2025, according to Expert Market Research.

The use of traditional and complementary therapies is not limited to India. In China, 89 per cent of publicly funded general hospitals at or above Grade II had traditional Chinese medicine clinics in 2023, according to Xinhua. Meanwhile, a nationwide survey by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation found that approximately 46 per cent of rural Indians and 53 per cent of urban Indians had used AYUSH systems to treat ailments.

These figures raise questions about how traditional and complementary practices can be integrated into healthcare delivery, and where they can complement conventional treatment without compromising patient safety or evidence-based clinical decision-making.

Against this backdrop, Namita Thapar, Executive Director of Emcure Pharmaceuticals and Founder of Arth, has partnered with Sir H. N. Reliance Foundation Hospital for a digital campaign focusing on integrative medicine and its role in patient care.

The campaign features Dr Tarang Gianchandani, Group CEO of Sir H. N. Reliance Foundation Hospital, who shared her perspective on the subject, “We should look at giving our patients the holistic care for which they trust us.”

The conversations feature doctors from different specialities discussing practices such as acupuncture, acupressure, Ayurveda, homeopathy, dance therapy, art therapy and music therapy, and their potential role alongside conventional medical treatment.

The campaign features the following doctors and healthcare leaders:

  • Dr Tarang Gianchandani, Group CEO, Sir H. N. Reliance Foundation Hospital
  • Dr Vaibhav Bagaria – Director, Orthopaedics & Joint Replacement
  • Dr Sewanti Limaye – Director, Medical & Precision Oncology
  • Dr Rahul Verma – Director, General Paediatrics, Neonatology, Paediatric Intensive Care
  • Dr Mukesh Thakur – Director, Acute Medicine & Clinical Transformation
  • Dr Firuza Parekh – Director, Well Women & Men Centre
  • Dr David Chandy – Director, Endocrinology & Diabetology
  • Dr Asha Dalal – Director, Obstetrics & Gynaecology
  • Dr Arun Shah – Director, Neurology
  • Dr Amit Maydeo – Chairman, Gastro Sciences

Speaking about the campaign, Namita Thapar said, “I think this is the future of healthcare, modern medicine and alternative healing working together. The purpose of this campaign is to show how top doctors across specialities are using integrative medicine to put the patient’s well-being at the centre of care.”

As interest in traditional and complementary therapies grows, their place in mainstream healthcare will depend on clinical evidence, appropriate patient selection and clear protocols for their use. The challenge for healthcare providers is to assess where these approaches may complement conventional treatment while ensuring that established medical standards remain central to patient care.
